pests.name: Birds
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Ripe and ripening berry clusters stripped from the shrub, often the whole crop in a few days as the fruit blackens.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Birds eating the berries, sometimes clearing a bush fast once the fruit ripens.
pests.cause_seasoned: Elderberries are a favorite of many birds, which are widely the number-one competitor for the crop.
pests.cause_beginner: Birds love ripe elderberries and are the biggest pest for the fruit.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Drape bird netting over the shrub or a frame before the clusters color, secured at the base. Cultivars whose cymes invert (droop) after fruit set, such as Bob Gordon, hide the berries and lose less to birds.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Cover the bush with bird netting before the berries darken, and tuck it in at the bottom. Some varieties (like Bob Gordon) droop their clusters and lose fewer berries to birds.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Net before ripening every season; harvest promptly and completely so ripe fruit is not left hanging. Scare devices help only briefly.
pests.prevention_beginner: Put netting up each year before the fruit ripens, and pick as soon as clusters are ready. Shiny tape and fake owls stop working once birds get used to them.

pests.name: Spotted-wing drosophila and sap beetles
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Small maggots inside softening ripe berries (spotted-wing drosophila), and small dark beetles feeding on overripe or damaged fruit (sap beetles); clusters ferment and leak.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Tiny maggots in soft ripe berries, or little beetles on overripe fruit, with clusters going mushy.
pests.cause_seasoned: Spotted-wing drosophila (an invasive vinegar fly) lays eggs in healthy ripe fruit; sap beetles are drawn to overripe and split berries.
pests.cause_beginner: A small invasive fly that lays eggs in good ripe berries, plus beetles that show up on overripe fruit.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Harvest ripe clusters frequently and completely, and remove fallen or overripe fruit (bag it, do not compost). Cool the harvest quickly. Monitor with apple-cider-vinegar traps.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Pick ripe clusters often and clean up any dropped or overripe berries. Chill the harvest fast. A cup of apple cider vinegar makes a simple monitoring trap.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Tight, frequent harvest and good sanitation are the core controls; do not let ripe or overripe fruit sit on the plant or ground.
pests.prevention_beginner: Pick often, keep the ground clear of fallen berries, and refrigerate promptly.

pests.name: Elder shoot and stem borers
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Wilting or dying individual canes and shoot tips; hollowed, tunneled stems, sometimes with sawdust-like frass at entry holes.
pests.symptoms_beginner: A cane or shoot suddenly wilting and dying, with a hollowed-out, tunneled stem.
pests.cause_seasoned: Native borers, including the elder shoot borer and the elderberry longhorned borer, whose larvae tunnel inside canes and shoots.
pests.cause_beginner: Beetle and moth larvae that bore into and hollow out elderberry canes.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Prune out and destroy wilted or infested canes below the damage as soon as you spot them; this removes the larvae. Keep plants vigorous and renew old canes.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Cut off and throw away any wilting, tunneled canes right away to remove the grubs inside. Keep the plant healthy and prune out old canes.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Annual removal of old and damaged canes during dormant pruning breaks the borers' cycle; destroy prunings rather than leaving them nearby.
pests.prevention_beginner: Prune out old and damaged canes each winter and get rid of the trimmings, which removes overwintering borers.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Clusters of small soft-bodied insects on tender shoot tips and leaf undersides, sometimes curling new growth and leaving sticky honeydew.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Tiny soft bugs on new shoots and leaf undersides, sometimes with sticky residue.
pests.cause_seasoned: Several aphid species feed on elderberry sap; heavy colonies distort growth and can spread viruses.
pests.cause_beginner: Small sap-sucking insects that cluster on new growth.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Knock light infestations off with a strong spray of water, support natural predators like ladybugs, and use insecticidal soap if needed. Avoid excess nitrogen.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Spray them off with water, let ladybugs help, or use insecticidal soap for heavy outbreaks. Do not over-fertilize.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Keep plants healthy without over-feeding, encourage beneficial insects, and inspect new spring growth.
pests.prevention_beginner: Do not over-feed, welcome helpful bugs, and check new growth in spring.

pests.name: Japanese beetles
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Skeletonized leaves (chewed to lacework between the veins), usually in early to midsummer, sometimes on the flower clusters.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Leaves chewed to lace by shiny beetles in summer.
pests.cause_seasoned: Adult Japanese beetles feed on elderberry foliage and flowers where the pest is established.
pests.cause_beginner: Shiny green-bronze beetles that eat the leaves in summer.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Hand-pick beetles into soapy water in the cool morning; a vigorous elderberry usually outgrows the damage. Skip lures, which draw more beetles in.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Pick the beetles off into soapy water in the morning. A healthy elderberry shrugs off most of the damage.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Tolerate light feeding on established shrubs; keep plants vigorous. Grub management in nearby lawn reduces local populations.
pests.prevention_beginner: A strong elderberry handles a few beetles fine; keep it healthy and pick off the worst.

diseases.name: Elderberry rust
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Bright yellow-orange spots and swollen, distorted growths on leaves, stems, and flower clusters; affected leaves may curl.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Orange spots and odd swollen growths on leaves and stems, with some leaves curling.
diseases.cause_seasoned: A rust fungus (Puccinia) that alternates between elderberry and nearby sedges as its other host.
diseases.cause_beginner: A rust fungus that moves between elderberry and nearby sedge plants.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Prune out and destroy infected shoots and clusters, and remove sedges growing near the planting to break the fungus's cycle. Good airflow helps.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Cut off and throw away the infected parts, and clear out any sedge weeds growing nearby. Keep the bush open and airy.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Site plants in the open with good air movement, keep sedges away, and remove infected tissue promptly.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Give the bush room and airflow, keep sedge weeds away, and cut out any infected growth you see.

diseases.name: Powdery mildew
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: A white to gray powdery film on leaves, usually late in the season; heavy cases can dull foliage but rarely harm an established shrub.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: A white powdery coating on the leaves, mostly late in summer.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Powdery mildew fungi, favored by crowded growth and poor air movement in late summer.
diseases.cause_beginner: A common leaf fungus that shows up on crowded plants in late summer.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Prune to open the canopy for airflow and remove badly affected growth; established elderberries usually tolerate it without treatment.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Open up the bush by pruning so air moves through. It rarely does real harm.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Space and prune for good air movement and avoid excess nitrogen that fuels dense, soft growth.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Keep the bush open and do not over-feed it.

diseases.name: Cane canker and dieback
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Sunken or discolored lesions on canes, with twigs and canes dying back, often on older or winter-injured wood.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Branches and canes dying back, with dark sunken patches on the stems.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Fungal canker pathogens that enter through wounds and stressed, old, or winter-damaged wood.
diseases.cause_beginner: Fungi that get into the canes through wounds or old, damaged wood and cause dieback.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Prune out affected canes well below the lesion into healthy wood, disinfecting tools between cuts, and remove the prunings. Keep plants vigorous.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Cut out dying canes below the damage, clean your pruners between cuts, and keep the plant healthy.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Renew old canes on schedule, avoid wounding, and keep the shrub vigorous and well watered.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Prune out old canes each year and keep the plant healthy so it resists infection.
